newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW - Bonn telecoms watchdog wants competition.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bonn telecoms watchdog wants competition.

text.p: Germany's new telecommunications regulatory chief, appointed this week by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet, said on Thursday his main focus would be to ensure a fair playing field for newcomers to the market.

Klaus-Dieter Scheuerle, the 42-year-old director of the Post and Telecommunications Ministry's regulatory department, takes up his new job on January 1, 1998, when telecoms markets in Germany and most of Europe are opened to full competition.
"All companies must have a fair chance to enter the competition," he told Reuters in an interview.
"The main point is that consumers should have more choice when ordering telephone service, that they are no longer dependent on the offer from Deutsche Telekom."

In the run-up to Wednesday's cabinet decision, Scheuerle's expected appointment was criticised by some who believed that as a civil servant he was too close to Telekom, the former monopoly in which the government still owns a majority stake.
The appointment of Scheuerle, a long-time aide to Post and Telecoms Minister Wolfgang Boetsch, was hotly disputed between the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and the centre-right government.

The SPD wanted to appoint Arne Boernsen, SPD member and head of parliament's postal committee. When that failed, they used their majority in the Regulatory Council to propose nominating Peter Landsberg, former chief of Alcatel SEL.
Responding to the criticism, Scheuerle said fears that he was too close to Telekom were "certainly without substance".
Until Wednesday, he had served on the supervisory board of Telekom's wireless unit Deutsche Telekom MobilNet GmbH.
But he described this position as an "emergency solution" after Telekom twice rejected other government candidates.
"We are the ones who abolished the monopoly of Deutsche Telekom," he said. "We have created legislation that in terms of its liberal orientation can stand up to international comparison."
It was important that the new Regulatory Agency be fair and independent in order to create a secure climate for investors.
"We want foreign investors to come to Germany and for local companies to invest as well. In light of the economic situation in Germany that is a very important aspect," he said.
Scheuerle rejected criticism from Telekom's competitors that Bonn was dragging its feet in implementing reforms so companies can prepare for full competition next year.

"I believe the tempo with which Germany has confronted these challenges has been breath-taking," he said, adding that it had been necessary to change Germany's constitution in order to privatise Telekom and this faced huge political resistance.

The Post and Telecommunications Ministry this week ordered Telekom to provide an offer by July 14 to competitors for so-called unbundled interconnection, which grants rival direct access to access lines of residential and business customers.

Telekom, which could face fines of up to one million marks, has appealed the decision and is also challenging an earlier ruling by the ministry regarding the fees it charges broadcasters for programme transmission.

The next likely battle between the regulator and Deutsche Telekom is likely to come over price-cap negotiations for 1998 phone tariffs. Telekom has not yet presented its rate proposals for approval. Scheuerle said it was too soon to comment.
